column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The article says Amin launched the 1972 invasion from Tanzania, but its own account (Obote's pilot, an uprising against Amin) shows the invaders were his opponents; worded without naming who led it.
The entry says some 2,500 labourers died; the article says only that historians estimate several thousand Indian labourers died. No figure given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has about 200 words of substance beyond a family list, and the entry already gives most of it
The article's 'Counterrevolution' section is garbled ('When the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata gained independence'); worded without that clause.

The entry is about urf as royal law in the Safavid Empire; the article treats the general Islamic term and says nothing of the Safavids. The text keeps to the general term and does not contradict the entry.

The article spells the temple both Wat Tha Thanon and Wat Tha Than; used Wat Tha Thanon. The article says nothing of the river port's role for the north or of Chao Phra Fang; nothing contradicts the entry.
The entry says he 'rebuilt his town' of Sabbioneta 'from the 1550s'; the article calls it a new city begun in 1556. Wording kept neutral ('a new town' is the article's).

The article also offers an alternative reading, that the stele may show a campaign to Cilicia (from the Anatolian-looking metal vessel carried as booty); left out, as the entry states the Lullubi victory as fact. The article's claim that Shutruk-Nakhunte descended from the Lullubi is left out as doubtful and unsourced in the text.
The article puts the beginning of open conflict in 753 yet also says Waiofar sacked Narbonne in 751 (Chronicle of Moissac); the Narbonne sack is left out.
The article does not name Pisa; it explains the Florentine crisis by English debts and the attempt on Lucca.

The article gives his dates as 1250-1337?; the entry gives only 13th-14th century, so no years are printed. The article's 'cycle of five linked pieces' is ambiguous (it may describe the orthodox repertoire or Wang's new form), so it is left out.

The entry dates Wang Mang's seizure of the throne to 9 CE; the article says 'In 8'. No year given for it in the text. The article calls her death in 'the spring of 13' while the lead gives 3 February 13; the lead's date is used, matching the entry's year.
The article calls the Genoese admiral at Chioggia Pietro Doria only in passing ('On the arrival of Pietro Doria, with reinforcements'); the entry names him as commander, so kept.

The article's lead oddly calls it a struggle between two claimants to the throne of Castile; left out. The article says John I was the successor of Henry II; it does not date the marriage, nor the final peace (the entry's 1375).

The article names the builder both Sri Dhammasokaraja and Si-Thamma Sokarat; the first is used. It says Si-Thamma Sokarat built the Mahayana-style Wat Phra Borom That when founding the city; the founder is not named in the text, as the spellings may stand for different kings.

The entry mentions Wilhelmstein and his military school; the article does not, so neither is repeated or contradicted. 'Died in infancy' rests on the article's dates: Emilie 1771-1774 and an unnamed son 1772.

The entry places Wilusa in north-western Anatolia; the article says western Anatolia. Neither is stated in the text. The article gives no date for the Alaksandu Treaty (only Alaksandu 'c. 1300 BC - after 1280 BC'), so none is given.
The article dates the agreement with Henry I over Kalisz to 1206 in one place ('treaty of 1206') but says Henry gave him Kalisz in 1207; only 1207 is given.
The kula ring and Malinowski are not mentioned in the article. The article's population of about 6,000 rests on an unofficial 2010 count; the 1990 census found about 1,700.

The article gives his death as 1036; the entry has 1035. The year of death is left out of the text. The article says his rule was marked by conflict with the Abbadids but does not say he was killed fighting them.

The article says the committee was formally founded at the Hôtel Madison in Paris on 30 April 1915 and designated London as its seat; the entry says it was founded in London. The place and day of founding are left out of the text.

The article places Yugra east of the northern Urals; the entry also includes the far north-east of European Russia. Location wording kept general. Al-Gharnati's account of Yura is already in the entry and not repeated.

The article places the town in the Ngaka Modiri Molema district; the entry says the Marico district. The district is not named in the text. The Bahurutshe and the revolt of 1957–58 are not in the article.
The entry says he joined the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1674; the article dates his invasion of Fujian to 1676. No year is given for the invasion in the text.
The article says accounts of his birth year vary (1595, 1600, 1604) but most agree on 1604; the variant years are left out.

The article dates the coup to 22 February 1921 (3 Esfand 1299); the entry has 21 February. The day is left out. The article says he spent about seventeen years in Europe before six in Palestine, yet has him elected in Jerusalem in December 1931; the length of the European years is left out. The British file quoted says he fell in June, the article 23 May; the text keeps 23 May. The article says he was elected governor of Yazd on his return; left out as doubtful.

The article says in its lead that the party was relaunched in 2008 by Michael Nkomo, but its sections credit Benny Ncube and Dumiso Dabengwa; Michael Nkomo is left out. ZIPRA's bases in Zambia (in the entry) are not in the article.
The article gives Basra's founding as 636 in the lead, 638 and 635 in the body; no year is given in the text.

The article's lead says Red Army soldiers freed them on 14 September; its body credits a commando unit led by Mikoyan. Worded to fit both. The lead's reason for the executions (letting the Islamic Army of the Caucasus take Baku) and the body's (the March Days) differ; no motive is given in the text.
Short article; the text uses nearly all of it beyond what the entry already says.
Short article. His death is not told; the last section only concerns the sarcophagus. 'Hunting alongside the eponymous general' read as Alexander.

The entry says he was killed in the fighting; the article says he disappeared and his ultimate fate is unknown. The text says only that he was last seen being evacuated and his body was never found. The article's body says he was elected Chairman of the Presidium in 1970, its lead gives 1978–1980 as head of state; the year of that post is left out.

The entry dates his execution to December 1818; the article to May 1819 (after six months in Cairo from November 1818). The date and the length of the Cairo stay are left out. The article attributes the Karbala desecration to 'the army of Abdullah bin Saud'; worded more generally.
The article dates his move to the Swedish navy to 1643 but says he left the French navy in 1644; neither year is given in the text.

The entry dates the meeting with Sonam Gyatso to 1586; the article to 1587 (and the khan title to 1587). No year is given for the meeting in the text. The article says Erdene Zuu was founded in 1585; the entry says around 1585. No year repeated.

The article has him marrying Tun Mutahir's daughter in 1860 in one section and his first wife Engku Chik, sister of Tun Koris, in Pahang in 1857 in another; the marriages are left out. The move of the capital and the 1895 constitution (in the entry) are not in the article.

The entry says he governed Fars and Khuzistan from 1024; the article has Khuzistan conquered by his vizier Bahram ibn Mafinna only after the failed attack on Basra of 1030. The conquest of Khuzistan is left out of the text for that reason. Jalal al-Dawla is called Sultan al-Dawla's brother, as in the article.

The article gives the Treaty of Petrópolis as ratified on 11 November 1903 in one place and signed on 17 November 1903 in another; the text says only 'that November'. The article dates the start of the siege of Puerto Alonso to 19 May 1902, before Castro's first action of 6 August 1902; the date looks like a slip and is left out.

The article gives the mosque as commissioned in 1373 and completed in 1375, but its terracotta section says it was built between 1364 and 1374. The text gives no years of construction; the entry's 1370s stands. The article calls it the largest mosque of the subcontinent at the time; the entry says among the largest, so the text makes no claim of size rank.
The article does not date the expedition itself; the entry's 26-25 BCE is left as it stands. His death is not told in the article, hence the heading Legacy.
The article names Salazar only as 'Dr. Salazar', so the text gives no full name.
The article dates the execution to 284 BCE; the entry gives d. c. 283 BCE. The text gives no year for his death. The article says the coins are of the 300 era; left out as unclear.

The entry dates the period from 1718 (the death of Charles XII); the article dates its start to the Instrument of Government of 1719. The text gives no start year. The article says the secret clause to uphold the Swedish constitution was in the 1772 Partition of Poland; the text says only that Russia saw the constitution as a means of subverting Swedish independence.

The article also mentions C. Garbini's 13th-century dating, dismissed by Edward M. Cook; left out for length. The article calls him a Phoenician King of Byblos in its lead but later says the inscription does not call him king; the text follows the later section and the entry, which does not call him king either.

The article says that at the end of the 19th century many Botocudo tribes still existed, numbering 13,000 to 14,000, but also gives Ehrenreich's 5,000 for 1884; the first figure is left out. The entry's raids on the captaincies of Ilhéus and Porto Seguro are not in the article and are not repeated.

The article says it was written between 1589 and 1596; the entry says completed around 1598. The text gives no date of writing. The article first calls the Mulk-Abadi the third book and then speaks of Todar Mal's Bandobast in 'this 4th book'; the text follows the five-book outline, which makes the Mulk-Abadi the third.
SKIPPED: the article has only about 200 words of history (Iwase Province, the Edo-period domain, Iwashiro Province) and otherwise a list of notable people; a longer text would be padding

The article says he was censured on 8 September 1937 'for being sufficiently vigilant', evidently a slip for insufficiently; the text says only that he was censured. The article gives the date of execution as 13 March or, in other sources, 15 March 1938; both are given, and the entry gives only the year.

The article dates Questembert to 888 or 889; the entry gives 888. The text names the battle without a year. The article calls him Duke of Brittany from 876; the entry has him count of Vannes and king from about 890. The text gives 876 only for Vannes and no year for the royal title.

The article lists his mother as Agnes of Cornouaille in the lead and as Orguen in the 1056/1060 charter (and his father as Eozen); the text names only Odo and Agnes in the first sentence and does not repeat the charter's names. The article dates the grant of Richmond both to about 1071 (lead) and to the Siege of York in late 1069 (Register of Richmond); the text follows the Register and gives 1071 only for the castle.

The entry dates his rule 369-358 BCE and his death to 358 BCE; the article gives c. 356 BCE, and Diodorus 357/356 BCE. The text gives no year for the murder. The article's lead names the murdered brother Polyphron and the reign section has Xenophon's and Diodorus's versions; the text follows the reign section.

The entry says it was uncovered in 1952; the article says its existence was first documented by French scholars in 1947, with Maslow's notes in 1948 and excavations in the following years, published in the 1950s. The text gives no years for the discovery.

The article gives the Qing conquest both as 1759 and as 'in the 1750s'; the text uses the 1750s for the conquest and 1759 only for the description of Dzungaria at that time, matching the entry's 1759. The entry's Khoja religious leaders and the Dzungar tribute from 1680 are not in the article and are not repeated.

The article gives several datings: modern sources 'between the sixth and the tenth centuries' or 'between the fifth and eighth centuries', Britannica the 7th to 10th centuries, Lochtefeld 7th to 10th; the entry says 6th to 9th. The text gives no century range. The article calls Nathamuni (824-924) a 9th-century theologian and also says he lived in the 10th century; the entry says he gathered the hymns in the 10th century. The text gives no date for Nathamuni.

The article gives the Mauritanian exile as 1903-1907 and also as five years; the text gives no years for it, and the entry gives none either. The article's 'beginning of the 19th century' for the French conquest of Senegal looks like a slip for the end of the century; left out. The present Khalifa-General named in the article is left out as a present-day detail.
The article does not say where she fled; the entry's Italy is not repeated or contradicted. Her death is not told, hence the heading Legacy.
The article dates the end of Âu Lạc flatly to 179 BCE; the entry says around 179 BCE, so the year is not repeated here.
The article contradicts itself on his accession: the lead says 1805 on his brother's death, the Reign section says Inthavong died in 1804. The entry's 1805 is not repeated; neither year is printed.
The entry speaks of frontier forts against the forest peoples; the article does not mention forts, so they are not told here.

The article dates the translation to 1793 in the lead and to 1794 later; the entry says 1794. The translation's year is not printed. The article gives his imprisonment after 1814 as six years and as four, and his return as 1820 and 1821; neither is printed. It also gives his escape at Cádiz as 17 March 1796 and his flight to Paris as 1795; neither year is printed.

The entry says he was born Anton Rösler; the article says many sources claim so, but Heinrich Phillip Bossler, who knew him, wrote in 1792 that he was named Rosetti from birth. The name question is left out of the text.
The article gives no Polykleitos statue; the entry's mention of it is not repeated. Thucydides dates the fire to 423 BCE in the article, as the entry does; the year is not repeated.
The article hedges her death at Samarra with 'if the early biographical information is correct'; the entry states it. Her death is not retold here.

The entry dates the annexation of Commagene to 72 CE; the article dates the war against Antiochus of Commagene to 73 AD. Neither year is printed for that war. The article treats his identification with the king of Armenia Minor as a scholarly identification; the text keeps that hedge.
The article does not mention the Ararat plain or the Araxes, nor the province named after the city; those are not repeated.

The article says the Don Army was part of the force from its formation on 8 January 1919, but its order of battle says the Don Army joined on 23 February 1919; the date of the Don Army's joining is not printed. The article does not mention the advance to Oryol; it is not repeated.
The article gives Harald Hardrada's reign as 1047 to 1066 in one place and from 1046 in another; neither is printed.
The entry says he received his lands in 1656; the article says the division was carried out on 22 April 1657. The year of the division is not printed.
The entry's figure of some 20,000 inhabitants is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article says Tuman Bay II was hanged on the orders of Selim II; the Ottoman conquest of 1517 was under Selim I, so the sultan's name is left out.

The entry says he became vizier in 1073; the article has him land in December 1073 and be named vizier after reaching Cairo on 27 January 1074. The year of his appointment is not printed. The article gives Atsiz's invasion of Egypt as December 1076 and as October 1076, and the Seljuk taking of Damascus as 1078 and 1079; neither is printed.

The article is short and partly lists; the text keeps close to it. Left out the article's present-day claim that Christians among them experience discrimination (a present-day assessment). The article does not mention upland rice, communal houses, missionaries or Mayrena (all in the entry).

The article says he served from 1796 (installed after Madhavrao II's death in 1795); the entry says he ruled from 1795. The year of accession is left out. The article states his date of death as 28 January 1851; only the year is used.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, most of it already in the entry
Later members listed in the article (the poet Ibn Zaydun, the physician Ibn al-Nafis) are left out: the article gives nothing on their link to the clan.

The article reports that medieval chroniclers have the Fatimids sending the Sulaym and Hilal west in 1050 or 1051 to punish the Zirids, but the historian Amar Baadj urges scepticism and attributes the migration to famine in Egypt. The entry states the Fatimid encouragement flatly, so the migration itself is not retold here; the editor may want to hedge the entry.

The article's list of kings dates Amary Ngone Sobel Fall to c. 1560-1593 and begins with Niokhor c. 1550, while its text makes Fall the first Damel-Teigne after Danki (1549); the dates of his rule are left out. The article also says Cayor invaded Baol around the turn of the 16th century under Teigne Mafane Thiaw, which sits oddly with the rest of its chronology: left out.
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, nearly all of it already in the entry

Birth year: the article gives c. 1836 (and 'around 1836-1838'); the entry has c. 1837. Left out. The article's lead has him ruling from 7 October 1870, its text says he succeeded Majid in 1871; the accession date is left out. It also calls both Majid and Barghash the second Sultan. The article dates the suspicion of taking slavers' money to the late 1860s, before his accession; the date is left out.
Birth: the article gives c. 1217/1219, the entry c. 1210. Left out.

His death is not told in the article, so the heading is Legacy. The years of the Dattus episode and the imperial march on Troia are given only relatively in the article (the year after 1020, the next year); left without years.

Birth: the entry has c. 925 (the Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium); the article also gives Brokaar's suggestion of 910-915. Left out. The article says the 3,000 armed attendants were 'according to the sources'; the entry gives the figure plainly, so it is not repeated.
The article calls it the Second Battle of Carabobo. Left out the article's own judgement on Bolívar's handing over of Miranda.
The article calls it a Spartan defeat of the Thebans and Argives; the entry calls the victory indecisive. The text tells the course and losses without judging the outcome.
SKIPPED: article about 260 words; too little beyond the entry for 260 words of text

The article says 83 of 95 Venetian ships were destroyed; the entry says the Genoese captured most of the galleys. Worded as 'lost' to avoid the difference. Article is short (about 300 words); the text stays near the minimum.

The entry calls Leslie's army larger; the article gives the English over 16,000 at the border and the Scots 12,500 or fewer at the battle, after the English had been weakened by disease. No comparison is made in the text.

The entry states as fact that the victory cut off the Britons of the south-west from Wales and opened the lower Severn valley to settlement; the article presents this as the traditional view (Guest 1849) that later scholarship questions. The text attributes both views; the editor may want to hedge the entry's last sentence.
The article dates the battle 18 June 1675 (Julian) = 28 June (Gregorian), as the entry does; the other day dates of the campaign are given in the article in the Julian calendar, so they are left out.
Skobelev's reported losses for the final day (59 killed, 304 wounded) left out for length.
The article's count of 427 years of Sasanian rule left out for length. The relief scene is described as the article does (Dad-windad called minister there, chief secretary elsewhere).

The article says the false order was purportedly given by La Mar in one place and that Razuri invented an order given by Bolivar in another; the text says only 'a false order'. Article spells 'Mayor' for Major; written Major. 'Four months later' in the entry agrees with 6 August to 9 December.
The article spells Roháč's seat both 'Dubá' and 'Dubé'; 'Dubá' used. The gloss of Wagenburg as a ring of wagons is implied by the article's account (fire from wagons).

Present-day money conversions of the article ('as of 2025') left out. The article does not name the Treaty of Berwick; it says David was released eleven years after the battle for 100,000 marks, which agrees with the entry.
The article calls Albert 'Albert, Duke of Burgundy' and 'the Archduke'; only 'the Archduke' used, in line with the entry's Archduke Albert of Austria.
The article gives the date also as 19 November in the lunar calendar; left out. Article's 'more than half of the 500 ships destroyed or captured' agrees with the entry's 'a large number'.
Article dates the battle 'September 1141' / 9 September 1141; entry says 1141; no conflict. Sanjar's wife was ransomed for 500,000 dinars (as Turkan-Khatun) per al-Husayni; left out.
The entry says the defeat contributed to French losses in India; the article does not mention India, so nothing on it is written.
The article spells the regent Theresa and Teresa and her ally both Fernão and Fernando Peres de Trava; Theresa and Fernão Peres used, in line with the lead.

The entry places the field in central Albania, the article near Lushnjë 'in modern-day southern Albania': the region is not named in the text. The article dates Balša's taking of Durrës 'by 1383 or 1385'; no year given. Article's '527 years' of Albanians in Ottoman service left out.
Article: 'early summer of 1167' and 8 July 1167, both consistent with the entry.

The article's lead says fighting broke out on 30 October after Mallaby was killed, while the body has the Indonesian attack on 28 October and the ceasefire and Mallaby's death on 30 October; the body's sequence is followed. Indonesian force figures differ inside the article (mobs of 70,000-140,000; 100,000-120,000 irregulars); left out.
Casualty figures differ by source (Shelby, McAfee, Bullock, Warburton and Evans); Harrison's report used and attributed. Indigenous dead: 16 by British count, 33 by Harrison's; left out.

The article reports Philip Dunshea's argument that Bede's phrasing allows the battle to have been fought some time, even years, before 15 November 655 and far from Leeds; left out because the entry dates it firmly to 15 November 655. Urbs Iudeu's identification with Stirling or Jedburgh left out as uncertain.

The article's sentence on Fort Bréda (on the habitation where Louverture worked as a coachman 'under François Capois') is garbled; only the fort is named. The article's 'paid until well into the 1900s' left out.

The article names only two of the men hanged in 1885 (Crooked Leg and Man Without Blood) and does not say eight were hanged together; the text does not contradict the entry's eight. Article says the NWMP fort and post office dates; the territorial seat 1878-1883 in Old Government House vs capital 1876-1883 in the entry: both kept as the article words them.

The entry says he became first chief minister in 1961 and prime minister under internal self-government in 1962; the article says self-government came on 1 March 1962 and he then became first Chief Minister. No year is given for his taking office. The NFL career of his grandson left out (a living person, not history).
The entry dates his birth c. 1360, the article 1360 without c.; no birth year is given in the text. The article is short (about 350 words, much of it already in the description).

Dates left out: the article dates the railings c. 125-100 BCE and the gateway c. 100-75 BCE, and reports Ajit Kumar and others placing the stupa in the 1st century CE; the entry says the stupa is of the 2nd century BCE, so no date is printed. Cunningham's remark blaming Muslims for the end of Buddhism left out.
The article's list of notable Bhutias (mostly living sportsmen and politicians) was left out.

The entry names the Chalukya capital Kalyani; the article calls it Kalyana: the city is not named in the text. The article's lead says the Kalachuri king was Lakshmi-karna; the body says Karna (r. c. 1041-1073). Text says Karna. The entry says Bilhana is credited with the Chaurapanchashika; the article calls the attribution doubtful, which the text says without contradicting the entry. The article gives 1087 'or early 1087' for the poem's completion; text says 1087.

The entry dates the Great Mosque to 1312; the article says the Aydınoğlu Mehmet Bey Mosque was commissioned in 1313: no year given in the text. The entry calls Birgi a small town; the article says it was a town (belde) until 2013 and is now a neighbourhood of Ödemiş. The text states the reorganisation.

The entry says he helped Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava repel the expedition; the article does not mention Eslava and speaks of forces under Lezo's command. The text avoids saying who held overall command. The article says the British withdrew 'in late May' while the attack ran to 20 May; text gives the attack dates and the withdrawal without a day. Left out: the many recent novels and the 2016 online poll.

The article calls the son who succeeded him Barnim XI in the text and Barnim IX in the list of children: the text gives no numeral. Nothing in the article on the administrative and financial reforms the entry mentions.

The entry places the Bono in west-central Ghana and eastern Côte d'Ivoire; the article says central Ghana and northeastern Ivory Coast: no region given in the text. The article says nothing of the Kingdom of Gyaman the entry mentions. The article's claims that many core Akan elements originate with the Bono were left out as one-sided.

The article calls the 1922 party the League of Communists of Yugoslavia (its later name); the text says 'the communist party' for 1922, as the entry names the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. Left out: the 2008-09 ownership dispute and the 2020 magazine's government support, to avoid present-day judgements.
The article is short (much of it a list of honours); the text keeps to about 290 words.

The entry gives the length as about 420 km; the article gives no length for the line as built (only the 530 km plan of 2010): no length in the text. Left out: the Fitch rating and the Lowy Institute's debt estimate (ratings and indices).

The article dates the division 'probably around AD 197' (Herodian's date) while the entry places it in the early third century: the text gives only the formalisation under Caracalla (211-220, probably c. 214), which the article also states, and leaves out 197. The article's lead says the subdivision lasted until 296; kept.

The entry calls Burghead a village, the article a small town: the text uses neither for the present place except 'the town' for its fishing past; editor may change. The entry dates the fort's occupation to the 4th-10th centuries; the article gives no dates for occupation, so none in the text.

The article says the MAN takeover was 'announced' in 1971; the entry says taken over in 1971: text does not repeat the year. The article's 1923 claim of 'the world's first full-size bus' was left out as unattributed.
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, much of it already in the entry (Phoebidas, 379 BCE, Macedonian garrison) or on the unrelated mineral cadmea; too little for a longer text

Alex Woolf's view that he was not of the Gwynedd line is given as Woolf's argument; the entry calls him king of Gwynedd, which the article's lead also does. Geoffrey of Monmouth's claims (Exeter, Penda's half-sister, survival to 654/655) are marked as legendary or left out.

The entry says the Russian Baltic Fleet anchored there in 1905; the article says the 40-ship Imperial Russian fleet under Rozhestvensky used it as a staging area: not repeated. Left out: the commentators' reading of the 2010 reopening as aimed at China, and Russia's 2016 talk of returning.
The article does not mention the lawsuits the entry names. Article calls Talavera archbishop of Toledo; title left out to keep to what is needed.

The article says those 'after the rejection of the latter's widow and son' invited him; 'the people of Ioannina' is an inference: editor may reword to 'he was invited'. Article mentions 'not long after Maurice died' without identifying Maurice: left out.

The entry calls Catawba a Siouan language; the article says only 'part of the Catawban language family': no family named in the text. The article does not mention Cofitachequi. Left out: the North Carolina casino litigation detail and the 'full-blood' discussion.
Short article (about 370 words); the text keeps to what it adds to the entry.
The article names Cedd's companions to the Middle Angles once as Diuma, Atta and Betti and once as Adda, Betti and Diuma; only Betti and Diuma are named here.

The article cites D. P. Kirby's view that Ceolwulf probably reigned into the early 880s; left out because the entry dates his reign to c. 879. The 877 division of Mercia is in the entry, not the article.
Sayce is given in the article without a first name or description.
The Kshatriya claims and the Bahujan Samaj Party are in the entry; told here only with what it leaves out.

The article calls Chandragiri a village; the entry calls it a town. The article does not mention the 1639 Madras grant or the Aravidu dynasty. A legend about nose rings taken from women in the fort was left out.

The article's lead says he governed from 1552 (he ruled Upper Baden in his father's name from September 1552); the entry gives 1553. The text gives both facts as the article tells them and does not date the start of his own rule.

The entry says Chen became acting head after Wang's death in 1944; the article says he was acting president of the Executive Yuan from mid-1944 while Wang was in Japan and became president on Wang's death in November 1944. The text says only that he was left in charge in mid-1944 and does not name his title after Wang's death.

The article also says the temple was destroyed by Malik Kafur in 1311 and Muhammad bin Tughlaq in 1326, which sits badly with its own account of damage recorded in 15th-century inscriptions and repairs; left out.
The article does not mention Kawali, its inscriptions, Cirebon, Mataram or Dutch rule; nothing here touches those points.
Antonelli's arrival in 1541 is as the article tells it.
The article's remark that Stalin 'departed from Marxism and drew on his own theological training' was left out as a judgement.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words; what it adds to the entry (family, the Bempflingen treaty, the Ulm charter of 1092, Hirsau donations) makes about 220 words without padding

The entry says the treaty ceded some 23 million acres; the article gives more than 21 million (21,086,793 acres) plus 1.9 million acres claimed by the Cherokee. No figure is given here. The article dates Floyd's camp at Callabee Creek to 26 January 1813, evidently a slip for 1814; left out.
The article says the castle was built around 1230 and first recorded in 1239; the entry says the 1230s. No building date is given here.

The entry says Ivan moved the seat to Cetinje in 1482; the article says he moved the seat of the Zeta Metropolitan from Prevlaka to Cetinje in 1485. The year is left out. The article is confused about Radič's sons Đurađ and Aleksa (called Đuraševići and said to have taken Crnojević lands); I kept only their rule of Upper Zeta as Venetian vassals from 1403, which the lead and the rulers list support. The article says Đurađ's descendants lived in Hungary and Venice, where they died out in 1660 with Ivan (Giovanni) Crnojević.
